claims.claim: Le Guin points to the broken monosyllables of Silas Marner's speech in George Eliot as an inseparable part of the passage's meaning.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Reciprocity of Prose and Poetry" (1983), in Dancing at the Edge of the World (1989)

claims.claim: Le Guin says of her own earlier novel The Lathe of Heaven that the characters talk too much and explain things too much.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin interviewed by Paul Morton, The Millions, 31 January 2013
claims.quote: They talk too much. They explain things too much.
claims.page: answer near the end of the interview

claims.claim: Le Guin says an irresistibly readable story can be told in the most conventional, banal prose if the writer has the narrative gift.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 51, "The Narrative Gift as a Moral Conundrum", 2011 (text at ursulakleguin.com)
claims.quote: An irresistibly readable story can be told in the most conventional, banal prose

claims.claim: Le Guin says art is not explanation but what an artist does.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 36, "Readers' Questions", 2011 (text at ursulakleguin.com)

claims.claim: Le Guin says that in writing Lavinia she was not choosing the way as an author but taking dictation.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin interviewed by Euan Monaghan, Literary Hub, 1 April 2016
claims.quote: I wasn’t choosing the way as an author, I was taking dictation
claims.page: answer on the origin of Lavinia

claims.claim: Le Guin praises Galt for telling without showing, in defiance of what she calls the decree of the Iowa Writing School.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.page: essay body, pull quote and following paragraph

claims.claim: Le Guin quotes the minister's entire account of the riot at his installation, which reads that he thought he would have a hard and sore time of it with such an outstrapolous people.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017, quoting John Galt, Annals of the Parish (1821)
claims.quote: a hard and sore time of it with such an outstrapolous people
claims.page: essay body, block quotation from Galt

claims.claim: Le Guin notes that the annalist moves from the riot to the dinner without even a period, only a semicolon.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.quote: without even a period, only a semicolon
claims.page: essay body, paragraph following the block quotation

claims.claim: Le Guin describes Galt's humour as dry, subtle, morally loaded, and really funny.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.quote: dry, subtle, morally loaded, and really funny
claims.page: essay body, paragraph comparing Galt to Austen

claims.claim: Le Guin says genre is a rich dialect that becomes a jargon meaningful only to an ingroup if it gives up connection with the general literary language.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, contribution on Virginia Woolf to "The stars of modern SF pick the best science fiction", The Guardian, 14 May 2011
claims.quote: it becomes a jargon, meaningful only to an ingroup

claims.claim: Le Guin says the way magic works in the Earthsea books is a matter of language and names and has rules.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Frankenstein's Earthsea", Locus, January 2005
claims.quote: a matter of language and names; it has rules
claims.page: essay body, on the film's changes

claims.claim: Le Guin says the rules of Earthsea magic give it a necessary limitation.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Frankenstein's Earthsea", Locus, January 2005
claims.quote: which give it a necessary limitation
claims.page: essay body, on the film's changes
